items.prompt: A marketplace stores orders, order lines and stock counts; placing an order must decrement stock for every line or for none, and stock may never go negative.
items.why: A multi-row atomic change plus an invariant (CHECK qty >= 0) is what ACID transactions and constraints are for.

items.prompt: A chat app stores 500 000 new messages/s; each conversation is read back newest-first, and there are no joins.
items.why: Huge append-only write volume with one access pattern (partition by conversation, cluster by time) is a wide-column store. A single Postgres primary's WAL can't take it.

items.prompt: A concert sells 50 000 seats; two buyers clicking the same seat at the same moment must never both get it, and support staff run ad-hoc queries on bookings.
items.why: A uniqueness invariant under concurrent writers (row lock, version column or UNIQUE constraint) plus ad-hoc relational queries → a relational database.

items.prompt: A shopping-cart service needs single-digit-ms reads and writes by cart_id at millions of requests/s, globally, with no cross-cart queries and no ops team.
items.why: A pure key-value access pattern at very large scale with zero operations → a managed key-value store. No joins or multi-row transactions are needed.

items.prompt: A payment service writes 1 000 payments/s; each payment creates balanced debit and credit ledger entries that auditors must be able to query and reconcile.
items.why: Moderate write rate, money and a cross-row invariant (debits = credits) → transactions on a relational primary. The scale doesn't force anything more exotic.

items.prompt: A dashboard shows p99 latency per service over the last 30 days from 2 million data points per second.
items.why: High-rate timestamped metrics queried by time range and downsampled → a time-series store. Row-oriented Postgres would bloat and scan slowly.

items.prompt: A job scheduler keeps 100M job definitions and every second must find the jobs whose next_run_at has passed, then claim each one exactly once.
items.why: A durable table, an indexed range query on next_run_at, and claim-and-advance in one transaction (SKIP LOCKED) play to relational strengths.

items.prompt: A game needs a live top-100 leaderboard updated 50 000 times/s; losing the last second of scores in a crash is acceptable.
items.why: In-memory sorted sets give sub-ms rank updates, and the relaxed durability rules out paying for a transactional database here.
